title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus
summary: Distributed systems face unavoidable trade-offs between consistency, availability, and latency. CAP and PACELC frameworks help you reason about these trade-offs consciously. Consensus algorithms like Raft keep replicas in agreement — powering everything from etcd to distributed databases.

sections.title: The Reality of Distributed Systems
paragraphs: When components run on multiple machines connected by a network, failures are normal — not exceptional. Networks partition, packets drop, nodes crash, clocks skew. A distributed system must continue operating (or fail gracefully) despite these failures.

The fundamental challenge is maintaining shared state across unreliable nodes. Should all replicas agree before responding (consistency)? Should the system keep serving requests even if some replicas are unreachable (availability)? You cannot maximize both during a network partition.

Understanding these trade-offs prevents you from choosing tools with wrong expectations — expecting strong consistency from an AP cache or five-nines availability from a CP coordination service during splits.

sections.title: CAP Theorem
paragraphs: CAP states that a distributed data store can provide at most two of three properties: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system operates despite network partitions between nodes).

In practice, partition tolerance is non-negotiable — networks fail. So the real choice during a partition is Consistency (CP) or Availability (AP). CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, traditional RDBMS with sync replication) may reject writes or reads to preserve consistency. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB with eventual consistency) accept writes on both sides of a partition and reconcile later.
CAP is often misunderstood as a static label. Systems can be mostly AP with tunable consistency, or mostly CP with read replicas that serve stale data. Context and configuration matter.

sections.title: PACELC Extension
paragraphs: PACELC extends CAP: if there is a Partition (P), choose between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), choose between Latency (L) and Consistency (C). This captures the everyday trade-off even when the network is healthy.

Even without partitions, synchronous replication to all replicas adds latency. Many systems default to reading from the nearest replica (low latency, eventual consistency) and offer optional linearizable reads (high latency, strong consistency) per request.

DynamoDB is PA/EL by default (available during partition, low-latency eventually consistent reads). PostgreSQL with synchronous replication is PC/EC (consistent during partition, consistent but slower when healthy). Cassandra is PA/EL with tunable consistency per query.

sections.title: Consistency Models
paragraphs: Strong consistency (linearizability): every read sees the latest write — as if one copy exists. Eventual consistency: replicas converge over time; reads may return stale data temporarily. Causal consistency: preserves cause-effect ordering without full linearizability.
Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own updates. Monotonic reads: a user never sees time go backward. These session guarantees are often sufficient and cheaper than global strong consistency.
Choose consistency per operation: financial transfers need linearizability; social media like counts tolerate eventual consistency; shopping cart reads need read-your-writes.

sections.title: Consensus with Raft
paragraphs: Consensus algorithms ensure multiple nodes agree on a value or log sequence despite failures. Raft is the approachable standard: nodes are followers, one leader is elected, the leader replicates log entries to a majority quorum before committing.

Quorum (majority of nodes) ensures any two quorums overlap — at least one node has the latest committed entry. Leader election uses randomized timeouts to avoid split-brain. etcd, Consul, and CockroachDB use Raft variants.

Consensus is expensive — typically 3 or 5 nodes, limited write throughput compared to leaderless systems. Use it for coordination (service discovery, config, locks), not high-throughput data ingestion.

deepDive.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus — Operational deep dive
paragraphs: Operating CAP, PACELC & Consensus well means defining the scarce resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, or tokens), the SLIs that reflect user pain, and the knobs that trade cost for latency.
Under load, measure amplification: how many bytes, RPCs, or disk writes you pay per user request. Prefetch and batch only when measurements show benefit — premature batching adds tail latency.
Failure drills should include dependency slowdown (not only hard down), clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts, dashboards, and runbooks against those drills.
bullets: Name the scarcest resource and budget it
Track p50/p99 and error rate for the user journey

deepDive.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus — Correctness edges
paragraphs: Correctness edges around CAP, PACELC & Consensus often appear at retries, partial writes, and schema evolution. Make handlers idempotent and state transitions explicit.

Document what clients may observe during failover: stale reads, duplicate messages, or delayed visibility. If the product cannot tolerate an anomaly, enforce a stronger consistency boundary — and pay for it knowingly.

expert.title: CAP, PACELC & Consensus — Expert / multi-region notes
paragraphs: At multi-region scale, CAP, PACELC & Consensus interacts with RTT, quorum placement, and cost of cross-region replication. Prefer region-local user paths with asynchronous global state when invariants allow.
Cost envelopes matter: chart unit cost vs QPS and vs data size. Many 'performance' projects are actually cost projects in disguise — make the objective explicit.

concepts: CAP: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — pick two during partition
PACELC: Latency vs Consistency when network is healthy
CP systems: etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner (with TrueTime)
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads session guarantees
Raft consensus: leader election, log replication, quorum
Split-brain: two leaders during partition without quorum
Fencing tokens to prevent stale leaders from writing
practices: Classify each data store in your architecture as CP or AP with PACELC
Use consensus stores (etcd) only for coordination, not bulk data
Request strong consistency only on operations that require it
Run clock sync (NTP/Chrony) on all nodes — skew breaks TTL and ordering
Test partition behavior with chaos engineering (iptables, toxiproxy)
Monitor replication lag on read replicas before serving stale reads
Use fencing tokens when relying on distributed locks
pitfalls: Labeling a system 'CP' or 'AP' without understanding tunable consistency
Using etcd for high-throughput writes — it is a coordination store
Assuming read replicas return latest data without lag monitoring
Ignoring clock skew in TTL-based leases and lock expiration
Split-brain from misconfigured quorum sizes (even number of nodes)
Choosing strong consistency globally when only one operation needs it

examples.title: Kubernetes etcd
examples.description: Kubernetes stores cluster state in etcd — a CP system using Raft. During a network partition, the minority partition becomes read-only. This is acceptable because cluster coordination demands consistency over availability. Application data lives elsewhere.

examples.title: DynamoDB global tables
examples.description: Multi-region DynamoDB global tables replicate asynchronously — AP with eventual consistency across regions. A user updating profile in US-East may see stale data in EU-West for seconds. Product accepts this for profile reads; payment uses single-region strong consistency.

examples.title: Bank transfer with quorum
examples.description: A bank uses a strongly consistent store requiring quorum writes for transfers. During partition, minority nodes reject writes — users see errors rather than double-spend. Availability is sacrificed for correctness on this critical path.

keyTakeaways: Partition tolerance is mandatory — the real choice is consistency vs availability
PACELC captures latency vs consistency trade-offs during normal operation
Match consistency level to operation criticality — not everything needs linearizability
Raft and quorum-based consensus power coordination services like etcd
Test partition and failure scenarios — theoretical CAP choices meet reality in production
Read replicas and caches introduce staleness — monitor lag explicitly
whyItMatters: Every distributed database, cache, and coordination service embeds CAP/PACELC trade-offs. Misaligned expectations cause data corruption, double-spending, and split-brain incidents. System design interviews center on articulating these trade-offs for specific requirements.
reflectionQuestions: Is Redis Cluster CP or AP during a network partition?
Why does etcd use Raft for Kubernetes instead of a simple key-value store?
When is eventual consistency unacceptable for your application?
How does PACELC apply to a read from a PostgreSQL async replica?
